shots.lineText: Sunlight looks white, so why is the clear sky above you blue and not white too?
shots.camera: slow push in over the whole video (zoom 1.00 to 1.05), eye level on the sea
shots.onScreen: empty day sky over a calm sea, sun upper right, a few clouds; nothing else, the sky carries the question

shots.lineText: White sunlight carries all the colours of the rainbow, so why does the sky pick out the blue?
shots.onScreen: a white beam from the sun opens into a rainbow fan on "colours"

shots.lineText: Each colour travels as a wave, and blue light travels in shorter waves than red light.
shots.onScreen: a long red wave and a short blue wave over the sky, each labelled as its colour is named
shots.text: RED · LONG WAVES / BLUE · SHORT WAVES

shots.lineText: The air above you is full of gas molecules, and all that sunlight has to pass through them.
shots.onScreen: gas molecules fade in across the sky on "molecules"; sunbeams fan out from the sun on "pass"

shots.lineText: Gas molecules scatter blue light in all directions more than the other colours, so blue reaches you from the whole sky.
shots.onScreen: molecules throw blue rings in every direction on "scatter", the sky deepens to a stronger blue

shots.lineText: Near the horizon the sky looks paler, because that light crossed more air and its blue was scattered many times in many directions.
shots.camera: camera sinks toward the horizon (eye point 820 to 1560 px, zoom +0.16) until the end
shots.onScreen: molecules and rays fade out; the horizon turns paler on "horizon"

shots.lineText: Send this to the next person who asks you why the sky is blue.
shots.onScreen: the pale horizon held under the share line, 3 s hold at the end
